newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Shareholder battle looms at Russia's Mosenergo.
newsitem.headline: Shareholder battle looms at Russia's Mosenergo.

text.p: Foreign shareholders will fight the management of one of Russia's most Western-looking firms, power utility Mosenergo, analysts said on Thursday, threatening the first such challenge to a major Russian company.

Mosenergo management will propose changes to the company's charter at the annual meeting on Monday which would limit the voting rights of big shareholders and authorise new stock that, if issued, would dilute capital by 30 percent.

Western investors, who own 34 percent of Mosenergo shares, oppose the proposals and the outcome could influence the entire stock market, which often follows the lead of Mosenergo, Russia's largest regional electicity utility.
"If the charter amendments are passed it is going to put a damper on the entire market," said ING Barings chief trader Peter Kizenko. "This could really shock some people."
Kizenko and Deutche Morgan Grenfell research chief Jim Nail said Mosenergo shares could fall to $1.00 or below, though the market has already begun to price in the foreigners' defeat on Monday.
Mosenergo shares had nosed up to $1.220 at midday on Thursday from Wednesday's $1.215 close on the Russian Trading System.
They fell to about $1.12 from $1.35 in the week after Mosenergo announced the proposals.
Nail, who along with another senior Western analyst said the foreigners would win, predicted shares could jump 10 percent if they blocked the changes.
To succeed they need 25 percent of the vote. But proxy voting rights for shares revert to management in some cases if not claimed, which could tip the balance in management's favor.

Mosenergo's main shareholder is Russia's national power company Unified Energy System which holds 49 percent of the stock. Workers and management own 11 percent, with six percent with domestic investors and the rest in foreign hands.
Mosenergo's proposals would increase authorised capital by 800 million shares from the current 2.6 billion and require board members to have 25 years experience in the power industry.
A final proposal would limit investor voting rights, regardless of holdings, to one percent of company total, without company approval.
Mosenergo has gone out of its way to lure foreign investors. American Depositary Receipts, share proxies bought on foreign markets and held mostly by Westerners, represent 25-28 percent of shares.
The company is considering issuing a level-three ADR, which would raise new capital abroad. It was one of the first Russian companies to launch an entry-level ADR and announce plans for a Eurobond.
These plans might suffer if foreign investors become disenchanted and its investor-friendly reputation is under threat.
"Mosenergo's much-vaunted outside-investor friendliness and sophistication was not evident," Renaissance Capital wrote after a meeting with Mosenergo management.
Gavin Rankin, research director at Troika-Dialog, warned that a significant dilution of investor's holdings could haunt Mosenergo if it wants returns to foreign markets for capital.
"They should take into account their poor attitude to shareholders rights if they are seriously considering a level three ADR issue," he said.
Others warned the desire to raise fresh capital spelled poor business and felt the attempt to limit voting rights amounted to a slap in the face.

"It is one thing to ask for a slush fund -- it is another at the same time to ask to put a tape over your mouth," said one Western investor. "They want to find new sources of funding to avoid working on a commercially effective basis."
